claims.text: Sleep log for several weeks, including bedtime events and use of medications, alcohol, caffeine, marijuana and nicotine.
claims.quote: Having patients keep a sleep log for several weeks is more accurate than questioning them. Bedtime events (eg, food or alcohol consumption, physical or mental activity) should be evaluated. Intake of and withdrawal from medications, alcohol, caffeine, marijuana, and nicotine as well as level and timing of physical activity should also be included.

claims.text: Ask about snoring, witnessed apneas, nocturnal gasping or choking, and nocturia (sleep apnea).
claims.quote: Snoring, interrupted breathing patterns, witnessed apneic events, nocturnal gasping and choking, and nocturia (sleep apnea syndromes)

claims.text: Bed partners can best identify some of these symptoms.
claims.quote: Bed partners or other family members can best identify some of these symptoms.

claims.text: Daytime sleepiness: Epworth Sleepiness Scale; a score of 10 or more means excessive daytime sleepiness.
claims.quote: The Epworth Sleepiness Scale may be used; a cumulative score ≥ 10 represents excessive daytime sleepiness.

claims.text: No testing needed when the picture clearly suggests restless legs, poor sleep habits, transient stress or shift work.
claims.quote: If symptoms or signs strongly suggest certain causes (eg, restless legs syndrome, poor sleep habits, transient stress, shift work disorder), testing is not required.

claims.text: Polysomnography when obstructive sleep apnea, narcolepsy, nocturnal seizures, periodic limb movement disorder or parasomnias are suspected.
claims.quote: Polysomnography is particularly useful when obstructive sleep apnea, narcolepsy, nocturnal seizures, periodic limb movement disorder, or parasomnias are suspected.

claims.text: Multiple sleep latency testing is mainly for diagnosing narcolepsy.
claims.quote: This test’s main use is in the diagnosis of narcolepsy.
